newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian opposition attacks Socialist government.
newsitem.headline: Albanian opposition attacks Socialist government.

text.p: The Albanian opposition on Friday accused the Socialist-led government of bearing political grudges and warned that a failure to abide by democratic principles could plunge the country further into instability.
Prime Minister Fatos Nano has vowed since winning an election in June to introduce sweeping institutional reforms and depoliticise the civil service.
The five-party coalition government has also promised to try to put the Balkan state back on its feet through the reform of the financial system, the police, and the army.
But in his first news conference since he resigned as president last month, Sali Berisha, leader of the opposition Democratic Party, accused the government of using the reforms for political revenge.

"We denounce the vengeful policies of the new officials in power which...are threatening stability, state institutions, democratic values and run contrary to the conditions stipulated by the international community," he said.
Berisha's party has formed a right-wing opposition alliance called the Union for Democracy with four smaller parties.
The government promptly rejected his criticism. "We are not involved in arbitrary dismissals," it said in a statement.

The international community pledged at a meeting in Rome last month to help Albania to rebuild itself, but warned that the new government must restore public order, improve human rights and adopt sound economic policies.
The collapse of shaky investment pyramid schemes earlier this year swallowed the life savings of Albanians, and triggered months of anarchy which led to the fall of Berisha's right-wing government.
More than 1,500 people have been killed in the former communist country since violence erupted in March, and security forces have yet to restore order in all parts of the country.

The newly-elected parliament is dominated by the Socialists and their allies with 119 seats in the 155-seat chamber. The Democratic Party, which won just 29 seats, is boycotting the assembly in protest against the handling of the election.
Berisha said Nano's government risked losing international support through its failure to adhere to democratic principles.
"There is an unshakeable will on behalf of the international community to assist Albania but we should fulfil its conditions," he said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton assured to Nano in a letter on Thursday of U.S. support for Albania's efforts to resuscitate its economy and restore order.
The International Monetary Fund and World Bank have outlined an extensive programme to help lift Albania out of its economic crisis and open the way to foreign investment.

A meeting of foreign ministers will be held in Rome in September and international donors are due to meet in Brussels in October to examine ways to provide aid to Albania in the form of approved projects.
